entry.title: whatis htop
entry.summary:
This is one of the tools that I use on a daily basis, and though sometimes I have to Google what these columns mean… ID of the process, like a unique identifier. Which user started the process. root – system-level daemon, syslog, etc – service users Priority. Lower number = higher priority. Kernel decides who gets CPU time first. Nice value. User-assigned priority tweak. Range: -20 (very important) to +19 (not so much). This exists to help us give priority to the process. Virtual Memory. Total memory the process can use. Includes swapped memory, shared libs, etc. In the image above, the numbers are in KB (kilobytes). Resident Memory. Actual RAM being used right now. This is the important one. In the image above, the numbers are in KB (kilobytes). Shared Memory. Memory shared with other processes: Shared libs Common system libs In the image above, the numbers are in KB (kilobytes).
So this means XX KB of the process’s memory can be shared with others.
S
What the process is doing now: S → Sleeping R → Running D → Uninterruptible sleep Z → Zombie We mostly see S because most processes wait for input.
CPU%
How much of the CPU the process is using right now. How much RAM it uses relative to total system RAM. Total CPU time a process has consumed since it started. The actual program that launched the process. Each has a story... Green Normal user processes Custom Python scripts, CLI scripts, etc. Blue Low-priority processes Red/Orange Kernel threads / High-priority tasks Cyan / Light Blue Threads inside a process (e.g., Python worker threads) Purple System daemons Bold Green Running processes Dark Gray / Dim Idle or sleeping processes taking almost 0 CPU
